title: Ash-e jow
subtitle: Persian barley and vegetable soup
excerpt: Ash-e jow is a thick Persian barley soup packed with vegetables, spinach, and chickpeas. Hearty enough to be a full meal, it is flavoured with turmeric, dried herbs, and finished with fried onion and dried mint. It is one of the most comforting dishes in the Persian winter repertoire.
sourceNotes: Ash (pronounced 'aash') is the Persian name for thick hearty soups. Ash-e jow means barley soup. This family of soups is central to Persian home cooking, particularly in winter.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well. The barley will continue to absorb liquid on reheating; add a little water or stock when warming.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Improves on day two. Keep refrigerated for up to 3 days.

content.text: Ash-e jow is the kind of soup that becomes a pot of comfort: thick with pearl barley, soft with spinach and chickpeas, and deepened with turmeric and dried herbs. It is a complete meal from a single pan.

The soup thickens considerably as it stands. Add a little extra water when reheating leftovers. The topping of crisp fried onion and dried mint stirred into hot butter is what lifts it from simple to special.
Pearl barley is the version to use here rather than pot barley; it cooks faster and gives a silkier texture. Tinned chickpeas are fine.

Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook for 8 minutes until golden. Add the garlic and turmeric and stir for 1 minute. Add the barley, chickpeas, stock, and salt. Bring to the boil, then reduce to a steady simmer and cook for 45 minutes until the barley is very soft and the soup is thick.
Stir in the spinach, parsley, dill, and lemon juice. Simmer for 5 more minutes. Taste and adjust the salt and lemon.

While the soup finishes, fry the sliced onions in the butter over medium heat for 15 to 20 minutes until dark golden and caramelised. Stir in the dried mint and fry for 30 seconds. Ladle the soup into bowls and spoon the crisp onion mixture on top.

rows.cause: Old barley or too low a simmer
rows.fix: Continue cooking for 15 more minutes with the lid on. Very old barley can take longer.

rows.cause: Barley absorbed more liquid than expected
rows.fix: Add water or stock in 100 ml increments until the consistency is right.

rows.cause: Under-seasoned or no lemon juice yet
rows.fix: Add the lemon juice and taste again; it lifts the whole soup considerably.

content.text: Add a swirl of strained yoghurt to each bowl for richness. Lentils can replace half the chickpeas. For a non-vegetarian version, a lamb bone simmered in the soup for the first 45 minutes adds considerable depth.
Ash-e jow is one of those soups that improves overnight. Make a day ahead and reheat, adding extra liquid if the barley has thickened it further. The mint-butter topping is best made fresh.

Ash is a category of thick Persian soups that spans dozens of variations and occupies a distinct place in Iranian food culture. Ash-e jow is among the most ancient, appearing in Persian cooking for centuries. It is winter food: filling, warming, and designed to sustain.
